posts.caption:
Everyone in China says ‘ecosystem, ecosystem, ecosystem.’ Foundery is a small attempt at trying to build that for consumer brands in India. It’s not about how many of the 20 brands per batch succeed or what valuations they achieve, but about the fact that, in 10 years, we would have built the rails and the ‘ecosystem’ by attempting to create 200 Indian brands with the potential to sell globally..

@jointhefoundery

Korea exported culture. 
Then the world bought Korean…

India has Bollywood, music, food, fashion, yoga and Ayurveda, a cultural moat very few countries can replicate..
Maybe we need to stop thinking only about exporting products and start deliberately exporting India. 
Consumer brands could follow.

The test of a first-rate intelligence is the ability to hold two opposed ideas in the mind at the same time, and still retain the ability to function.” — F. Scott Fitzgerald

The internet increasingly rewards the angrier, louder side, the more certain-sounding side, often the stupider side.

Maybe intelligence is being able to understand why the other side believes what it believes.

Introducing WTF: Discourse.

Two opposing ideas. Two people who actually believe them. No winner. Just the strongest version of both arguments.

You decide what you believe.
Did a travel episode, lots of insights and opportunities in this, basic premise was how to get the no of foreign visitors in India to go up from 10 million, but also what to build, live now

India gets about 10 million foreign tourists a year.

Dubai gets 18 million.

Dubai is basically one long road. We are 1.4 billion people with the Himalayas, Goa, Rajasthan, Kerala, the Andamans, 5,000 years of history and arguably the best food in the world :)

Something doesn’t add up.

Two men who built India’s biggest travel and hotel businesses agree on one thing: the country is easy to leave, hard to visit.

India has transformed dramatically over the last decade, better roads, airports, digital infrastructure and connectivity. Maybe tourism is the next big opportunity.

In this episode, the CEOs of MakeMyTrip and IHCL (Taj Hotels) tell us 5 things that could get a lot more of the world to come visit India, and where the opportunities for entrepreneurs might lie along the way.

Episode out now..

WTF Offline.

1 stadium. 10 hours. 150 people

No cameras, no press, no phones.

No audience either. Just friends and people I have had on the podcast over the years.

A safe space for conversations to happen differently when there’s no camera to perform for.

PS: We capped it at 150 people, partly to keep it intimate and partly because 151 onwards it starts to sound like the beginning of a cult :)

Travel inwards can bring in forex, jobs, and a lot of growth: a little more budget allocation, a slight tweak in attitude, a realisation that atithi devo bhava is better practiced than recited, like most other things in life. We all touch MakeMyTrip and Taj Hotels as Indians at some point. The two of them break down business opportunities and 5 things that need to change structurally.

Coming soon..
Interesting insight: smart foreign money isn’t always right, it’s often wrong, in terms of timing Indian stock markets. Foreign institutions vs. domestic: domestic seems to have done better...
Highlight of 2026, this ball going in when Diyaan was partnered up with his tennis coach.

Some days you build. Some days you watch other people build better than you. Both are good days. :)

@jointhefoundery @juspay.io @idfcfirstbank @experiencebroadway_

In FY2026, 31 lakh Indians chose to earn through Zomato and Blinkit as delivery partners. That’s 57% more than the previous year.

Behind every one of these numbers is a person with interests and ambitions. A student balancing classes, an entrepreneur building something of their own, a dancer pursuing their passion, and a parent juggling work and family.

We just completed a successful flight for our tech demonstrator, Lat One v0.2.

Lat Aerospace is building ultra-short takeoff and landing aircraft using blown wing technology. Think fixed-wing performance with near-helicopter access.

A couple of months ago, v0.1 achieved uSTOL but crashed shortly after. That was expected. v0.2 was about completing the full mission, and it did. The blown wing concept worked in reality. Closed-loop control got validated. We'd predicted a cruise speed of 30-32 m/s and cruised comfortably at 33. No thermal issues despite a burning afternoon. The quick-detach wings held through aggressive turns. Was in the air for over 6 minutes. Smooth touchdown, and ready to fly again.

But the thing that makes me the happiest isn't any of that. It's that our CFD studies, aerodynamic models, SIL simulations, and flight logs all match, almost perfectly. That's what real engineering looks like. I am so proud of our team.

A long way to go, and we are getting there.

posts.caption: Everybody is jealous of the destination. Nobody is jealous of the journey.

5 money rules my wife and I follow as a couple aged 45 with two kids.

1. We don’t spend money to look rich. 

We spend to become wealthy and gain freedom of our time.

So, there’s no car. It’s rented. 
We own the house we live in, no other real estate.

No spending on brands. No spending just to show off to people.

2. We spend extravagantly on high-quality food.

We know that what goes into our body is ultimately the biggest wealth we have, and unfortunately, healthy food is not cheap.

3. We spend on experiences more than things.

Things give you happiness once, and they have no end.

You remember experiences, and they make you a better person. 
You grow as a person.

We travelled 116 days last year!

4. We invest before spending.

As soon as our salary comes, the largest amount is invested.

The remaining amount is used for expenses.

We are recording this on the 30th. 
₹9,000 and ₹600 left in our bank accounts. 
Everything else is invested.

5. No budget for books and learning.

No amount of money spent is enough.

Ruchi is learning pottery, watercolor painting, and tennis.

Sometimes, the biggest thing holding you back isn’t your talent, your circumstances, or the opportunities you get. It’s the identity you’ve built around yourself.

If you believe you’re someone who always gives up when things get difficult, you’ll find reasons to quit. If you believe you’re someone who isn’t good enough, you’ll hesitate even when an opportunity is right in front of you. And if you’ve convinced yourself that a certain level of success is all you deserve, you might unconsciously stop yourself from going beyond it.

Not because you lack the ability, but because your actions are constantly trying to stay consistent with the person you believe you are.

That’s why real growth begins when you stop asking, “Am I capable of doing this?” and start asking, “Who do I need to become to make this happen?”

You don’t become confident and then take action. Sometimes, you take action while you’re scared, and that’s how confidence develops.

You don’t become disciplined overnight. You build discipline every time you keep a promise to yourself, especially when nobody is watching.

And you don’t become successful by waiting until you feel like a successful person. You become one by making the decisions, accepting the discomfort, and doing the work that your future self would be proud of.

Your current identity is often built from your past experiences, failures, fears, and the opinions you’ve accepted about yourself. But your past is evidence of what you’ve experienced, not a limit on what you can become.

So, stop using your current version as proof of your future potential.

You are allowed to outgrow the person you’ve been. You’re allowed to change your standards, challenge your old beliefs, and become someone your past self wouldn’t even recognise.

Your potential is not the problem. The way you see yourself might be.

Start becoming the person who can handle the life you keep dreaming about.

I keep saying this: for any regulated business, the biggest risk is regulatory risk. Today’s IRDAI draft on insurance commissions is a good reminder.

Broking is no different. A change in rules around retail F&O trading, how brokers can earn on client float, MTF requirements, or any of several other areas can change the economics of the business almost overnight.

So when valuing regulated businesses, you can’t just extrapolate current revenues and profits into the future. One regulation change can alter the economics, and the stock price along with it.

Pretty much everything in fintech comes with this risk 😬

People need to be able to close an account as easily as they open one, if not easier. Making it easy to open an account but impossible to close one is the oldest dark pattern in the book.

I think we are one of the few apps where the account closure option is clearly visible.

We (@zerodhaonline) close around 15,000 to 20,000 accounts every month for reasons ranging from company policies and trading losses to moving to another broker.

It might sound counterintuitive, but allowing customers to close their accounts easily is the mark of a good business.

posts.caption:
My number one piece of advice for anyone thinking of starting a business? Find a mentor (and actually lean on them).

When I was young, I had no trouble asking people for help. If someone had done something I was trying to do, I would pick up the phone and ask how they’d gone about it. I didn’t think of that as finding a mentor. I was curious, perhaps a little naive, and I knew there was a great deal I didn’t know.

Starting @VirginAtlantic brought that realisation to 30,000ft. I loved the idea of making flying better, but I had never run an airline. So, I reached out to someone who had - Sir Freddie Laker. He (very generously) gave me his time, told me what he had learned from building Laker Airways and spoke frankly about what they had gotten wrong. For example, he was extremely clear-eyed about the challenges we would face from our competitors. When British Airways tried to destroy us with their Dirty Tricks campaign, Freddie’s wisdom was invaluable. He helped us make decisions when the stakes were high, and he became a trusted friend along the way.

Over the years, I’ve learned from all sorts of people. My parents shaped the way I approached life long before I started a business. My sisters were my sounding board in the early days of Student Magazine. Freddie helped me when my head was above the clouds. Their mentorship was invaluable, and I’m not sure where I’d be right now without them all. 

One of the key reasons we started @VirginStartUp was to provide mentorship. In the lead up to National Mentoring Day on October 27, the team will be sharing some mentoring opportunities with some of the biggest founders and industry leaders in the founder world. Rare opportunities like this are there to be seized - this is what being a founder is all about. To get involved, join more than 4,000 founders on the Virgin StartUp Digital Community - a platform for practical support, mentorship opportunities, and networking events. Find all the deatils at @VirginStartUp's link in bio.

The brave may not live forever, but the cautious do not live at all. 
 
I wrote this in one of the first editions of Student magazine. They are words that have shaped my entire life.
 
Wonderful to see them plastered to the walls of @Virgin’s new office in New York - encouraging the team to make bold decisions and see where it takes them.

In my experience, the best businesses start by looking at an industry and asking: how could this be done better? 
 
This is our exact ambition with cross-Channel rail. Today, we shared a first glimpse of the bold black and red livery planned for our fleet of 12 @Alstom Avelia Stream trains. 
 
@Virgin's ambition is to run 20 daily return services between London and continental Europe from 2030. We want to bring more choice, some healthy competition, and more capacity to one of Europe’s most important travel routes. 
 
There is a huge opportunity here. More people are choosing rail for shorter journeys across Europe, and we believe Virgin can help grow that market by creating an experience people genuinely look forward to. After all, this is what we do best. 
 
We’ll bring together the best ideas from all across the Virgin family: from @VirginAtlantic’s distinct hospitality, and @VirginVoyages’ award-winning dining experiences, to @VirginHotels’ design approach, and everything we learned from 20 years of Virgin Trains. 
 
Exciting times ahead!
Our Mile High Tea has fans in high places ✈️

New York is always buzzing during Climate Week and the United Nations General Assembly. I come each year for the same reason: to have serious conversations that lead to meaningful change. 

Weeks like this aren’t about one person, one organisation or one big speech. They’re about showing up, listening, sharing knowledge and working together to turn ideas into action.

There are no easy answers to the challenges our world faces but spending time with so many brilliant, determined and hopeful people reminds me that progress is possible.

We all want to leave the world in a better place for our children and grandchildren, and the best way to do that is together.
Hanging out with @CorneelKoster and some of the @VirginAtlantic team at HQ. Meeting our teams is one of my favourite things to do.

So touching to see @VirginAtlantic’s new plane paying tribute to my wonderful wife, Joan. 
 
Joan was part of the Virgin Atlantic story from the very beginning. From joining the inaugural flight in 1984, to coming up with the idea of donating loose change on-board for charity (which resulted in almost every airline in the world following suit and raising billions over the years). She was always there. 
 
Seeing the details of our family tartan, the heart-shaped necklace, and the rings she wore every day, brought back so many happy memories.

We get one go at this life. Don’t spend it wondering, “What if?”
 
The best things in my life began before I knew what I was doing.
 
Saying 'yes’ has changed my life. It’s opened up doors. It’s forged friendships. It’s taught lessons that will never leave me.

The week I spend in New York for #Goalkeepers2030 and the UN General Assembly is always a highlight of my year. Last week was no exception.
At #Goalkeepers2030, I spoke with Archbishop Vicenzo Paglia about how people and relationships must remain at the center of how we use AI.

We have an opportunity—and an obligation—to ensure that AI tools are designed to improve lives and reach the people who stand to benefit most, including farmers, teachers, and health workers.  

Progress doesn’t happen on its own. It happens because the world invests in and prioritizes it. If we can combine increased generosity with the smart use of AI, there’s no limit to the progress we can make.

I’m the founder and CEO of Thrive Global, a behavior change technology company with the mission of improving health and helping us move from merely surviving to thriving. I also founded The Huffington Post and have written 15 books, including Thrive and The Sleep Revolution.

I’m originally from Greece (and still have the accent to prove it!). When I was 17, I moved to England and studied economics at Cambridge University, where I frankly spent most of my time debating at the Cambridge Union.

I live in New York but also spend time in Los Angeles, and love being a Yiayia (Greek for grandmother) to my almost three-year-old grandson Alexander and his newborn sister Annabel.

My journey to focusing on health began with a fall. In April 2007, I collapsed from exhaustion and burnout and hit my head on my desk on the way down, breaking my cheekbone.
 
In the wake of my fall, I found myself going from doctor to doctor to find out what was wrong. Doctors’ waiting rooms were good places for me to ask myself a lot of questions about the kind of life I was living.

After all the tests, it turned out nothing was wrong. Except for the fact that everything was wrong. I was suffering from an acute case of burnout. I had bought into the myth that burnout was the price I had to pay for success. 

I became more and more passionate about the five daily habits that drive so much of our health: nutrition, exercise, sleep, stress management and connection. That led me to write Thrive and The Sleep Revolution. 

The books struck a chord, but I wanted to go beyond speaking and writing to helping people move from awareness to action. So in 2016 I founded Thrive Global, which helps people transform their health by combining Microsteps — small, science-backed daily steps — with technology, storytelling and community. And last year, with the OpenAI Startup Fund, we launched Thrive AI Health to build an AI health coach to democratize access to health coaching.

posts.caption:
Today is World Mental Health Day. And we’ve made great progress in recent years raising awareness and opening up the conversation about mental health.

This year, I hope we take it one step further: mental health is brain health. A growing body of research shows how our brain health connects to everything from daily brain fog and anxiety to long-term cognitive decline.

So here’s a Microstep to try today: take a moment to check-in with your own mental health by naming the feeling you’re having right now in one word. Simply putting a feeling into words can help calm the brain’s stress response.

It might be “overwhelmed.” Or “tired.” Or “uncertain.”

Whatever it is, naming it is a small way to build the muscle of self-awareness, one of the most powerful tools we have for our mental and brain health.

AI keeps pulling off things that used to be impossible. In my latest On My Mind newsletter, I write why we shouldn’t lose sight of the eight “wonders of life,” as coined by @UCBerkeleyOfficial professor Dacher Keltner, that create everyday moments of awe: moral beauty, movement, nature, music, visual design, spirituality and religion, big ideas, and life and death.

Plus, dispatches from @Dreamforce, the @LucasMuseum, and my own home, where I recently hosted an event that captured the possibility of this moment when it comes to brain health.

You can read my newsletter at the link in bio.

Wise words, whether we’re elite athletes competing at the highest levels or building healthy habits in our daily lives. Congrats to @CaitlinClark22 — @WNBA Comeback Player of the Year! — on a great season, and thank you for your deep commitment to helping people live healthier lives by putting a spotlight on healthy behaviors, including the role of exercise as one of the most powerful preventative medicines, and reminding us all to start how we can.

@OpenAI solved a problem mathematicians have wrestled with for a quarter century.

@GoogleDeepMind mapped every possible mutation hiding in our genes. These are awe-inspiring feats of the machines.

In my latest piece for @time, I write about why, even as we marvel at AI’s capacity, we shouldn’t lose sight of something irreplaceable: human-generated awe.

Dacher Keltner, professor of psychology at the @ucberkeleyofficial, looked at 2,600 stories of awe across 26 countries. He found that what most commonly led people to feel awe wasn’t nature, or spirituality, or technology — it was watching other people be kind, brave, or strong.

He calls it "moral beauty" and 95% of it comes from witnessing actions people take on behalf of others. Collective movement. Nature. Music. Visual design. Spirituality. Big ideas. Life and death. These are the other wonders Keltner found that inspire awe — and they’re all deeply shaped by human connection.

AI will keep astonishing us. But the awe that has the most profound impact is the awe we derive from each other. And as Keltner writes, that awe is available to us "if we just take a moment and wonder."

You can read my full piece at the link in bio.

What a beautiful story of hope in The @Guardian. Twenty-one years ago, a field in Norfolk was home to a single crop. Today, it is a wildflower meadow with more than 150 plant species. Since 2011, the only maintenance has been one hay cut each summer. The cut keeps the field from becoming woodland and gives more delicate wildflowers room to grow.

As @UCL Professor Carl Sayer put it: “Sometimes we’re not patient enough.” And after watching the meadow become more biodiverse each year, he says, “It’s hope — we can recover things. We just need to do less in the recovery process.”

Life is a dance between making it happen and letting it happen. In this meadow, making it happen means one simple act of care each year. Letting it happen means trusting nature and giving it time. The same is true in our lives: our daily choices around sleep, food, movement, stress and connection give our bodies and minds the support they need to renew.

Read more in The Guardian at the link in bio.

Congratulations @ArielEmanuel on the publication of Roll the Calls!

Of course I knew Ari had an amazing story. Angry boy from Chicago overcomes severe dyslexia, rises from mailroom to C-suite, transforms himself into one of the legendary dealmakers and visionaries in Hollywood history – I expected Ari’s memoir to be a page-turner. But I didn’t expect such tenderness, such sweetness, so much heart. I wasn’t ready for all the wisdom about mental health and self-confidence and resilience and the search for one’s true happiness. I simply wasn’t prepared for Shoe Dog meets Goodfellas with a dash of The Little Prince. What a pleasant, refreshing, and wonderful surprise this book is.

Looking back at two great days at @Dreamforce. @Salesforce’s chief marketing officer @ErinOles moderated a conversation with @officiallymcconaughey and me about who shapes culture in the age of AI.

Here’s what nobody wants to admit about the content explosion: the bottleneck was never production. It was always judgment. For most of history, we assumed the hard part was making things — and the machines have now solved that. Anyone can generate a screenplay, a song, a strategy deck in seconds. But Matthew put his finger on what the machines haven’t solved: AI can tell you what’s popular, but it doesn’t yet have an ear for what’s really good.

Those are profoundly different things. Popularity is a pattern in the data. Good is a judgment — and judgment is built from everything that never shows up in training data: taste formed over decades, failures metabolized into instinct, the thousand small refinements of a lived life. Erin compressed it into one line: the real AI superpower isn’t the tool, it’s the taste.

Which means we’ve been worried about the wrong scarcity. The scarce resource of this era isn’t intelligence — machines have made intelligence abundant. It’s wisdom. And here’s the inconvenient truth about wisdom: it can’t be generated, downloaded, or scaled. It has to be lived into existence, one experience at a time.

Machines gather knowledge exponentially. Humans gather wisdom slowly. Whether that gap becomes a crisis or a renaissance depends entirely on whether we treat our own development as seriously as we treat the technology’s. And keeping people at the center of the AI conversation was the focus of my session at Dreamforce with chief people officer Nathalie Scardino and HR leaders from around the world.

A beautiful evening celebrating the opening of the @LucasMuseum of Narrative Art — a museum as expansive, surprising and impossible to categorize as the works it celebrates.

The museum houses the art collection of George Lucas and @MellodyHobson. At a time when AI dominates our public conversation, it’s a reminder that machines aren’t the only ones producing wonders. It’s a cathedral of wonder and awe, human creativity, storytelling and connection. As Mellody said, “Narrative art creates an emotional connection, not an intellectual one.”

The museum looks, appropriately, like a spaceship, rising, curving and folding into the landscape – in fact, there isn’t a right angle anywhere in the building. Works associated with empires and religious traditions live alongside illustrations, comic strips and movie images that have shaped our lives. There is even an immersive reproduction of the Sistine Chapel ceiling, which George calls “God’s comic book” because its panels tell a story. And throughout, cinema is treated not as something separate from art history but as another chapter in our ancient drive to turn experience into narrative. It’s why one of the museum’s theaters is named for Robert Flaherty, a pioneer of documentary filmmaking.

And then there are the monsters. The museum’s exploration of them brought to mind what Guillermo del Toro’s work shows about monsters being revealing mirrors. We create them to give form to what frightens us and to explore the parts of ourselves we can’t always confront directly. The same is true of the myths, which let us wrestle with the same big questions at a larger scale. The characters and settings change but the elemental questions remain: Who are we? What do we fear? What are we willing to fight for? And who can we become?

At a moment when so much is pulling us apart, George Lucas and Mellody Hobson have created a home for the images, stories and myths that unite us — a place where art is an invitation to feel, wonder and see ourselves in one another.

As we mark World Alzheimer’s Day, more than 7 million people over age 65 in the US are living with Alzheimer’s disease — a figure that is projected to almost double in the next few decades. And more than 12 million people are caregivers to loved ones with Alzheimer’s or other dementias. There’s no sugarcoating a disease that results in the widespread loss of brain function, and no number that captures the heartbreak of seeing a loved one decline. And yet, there is reason for hope.

That’s because research shows that Alzheimer’s-related brain changes can begin up to 20 years before symptoms set in, highlighting the importance of investing in our brain health and addressing modifiable risk factors throughout adulthood.

This is a 20-year window of opportunity. As with so many chronic conditions, research is showing that with brain health, our DNA is not necessarily our destiny. We have more power than we previously thought to shape our brain health, both day-to-day and in the long run.

posts.caption: My hope for the future? That every woman—no matter who she is or where she lives—can step into her full power because she’s able to get the care she needs.

If you want proof that our health systems overlook women, just look at menopause. It affects half the population, yet it remains poorly understood and drastically underfunded, leaving women without the care and relief they need. 
 
In The New York Times, I share why I’m directing new funding to raise the standard of care for menopause and perimenopause—and what it will take to unlock a menopause revolution. Read the full piece at the link in my bio.

Unlocking women’s power changes everything.
 
In our homes. 
In our workplaces. 
In our communities. 
In the rooms where laws are passed. 
And at the tables where decisions are made.

If you want to know what determination looks like, meet Shabana Basij-Rasikh.
 
Shabana was six years old when the Taliban first seized power 30 years ago and banned girls in Afghanistan from attending school. Undeterred, she continued her education in secret schools across Kabul, then went on to graduate magna cum laude from Middlebury College in Vermont and earn a master’s degree in public policy from Oxford.
 
But Shabana didn’t stop at pursuing her own education. While still in college, she co-founded @sola.afghanistan, Afghanistan’s first boarding school for girls, which attracted students from nearly every province in the country.
 
When the Taliban returned to power in 2021, they shut girls out of the classroom once again. Yet Shabana fought to keep her school alive, leading the SOLA community’s evacuation to Rwanda.
 
In the years since, the Taliban have enacted a brutal campaign against women’s rights, barring them from universities, most jobs, traveling without a male relative, and even speaking and singing in public. But Shabana has not given up on her mission. SOLA continues to educate Afghan girls in exile from its campus in Rwanda, and it reaches girls in Afghanistan through online learning.
 
I’ve been honored to get to know Shabana through Pivotal’s Global Leaders initiative, which provides visionary changemakers with funds to support work they believe in, and I couldn’t think of a more important person to interview for International Day of the Girl. She knows exactly what’s at stake when girls are denied an education—and what’s possible when they can get one.
 
Read my Q&A with @sbasijrasikh at the link in my bio. #internationaldayofthegirl

Margaret Hamilton was an extraordinary woman. One of the first programmers on the Apollo mission, she helped Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin safely reach the moon, coined the term “software engineer,” and inspired countless other people to break barriers in STEM.
 
She was also a mom. And with the news of her passing, I find myself thinking about a story I once read about her:
 
Margaret sometimes brought her daughter Lauren to work at NASA. One night, Lauren pushed a button that made the system crash. Margaret immediately realized that an astronaut might inadvertently do the same thing, so she recommended adjusting the software. 
 
Margaret’s bosses ignored her advice. But during the very next mission, the astronauts made the exact same mistake her daughter did. “After that, they let me put the program change in,” she said.
 
What a powerful reminder of the unique perspectives that parents bring to the table. That breakthroughs and discovery can come from unexpected places. That all around us, unsung heroes are working quietly and faithfully to expand our idea of what’s possible.
 
Thank you, Margaret, for encouraging us all to soar.

I grew up during a time when the workplace was built around a pretty narrow idea of who belonged and who could lead—which more often than not meant men. We still see the relics of that old reality in our workplaces.  
  
That’s why @pivotaldotcom and the @aspeninstitute teamed up last year to launch the @aspenwinchallenge, a $60 million initiative to remove barriers that prevent people from reaching their full potential—and finally bring workplaces into the future.  
  
Today, I’m excited to announce the 18 awardees. Their extraordinary ideas are reimagining what better workplaces could look like for everyone, and I can’t wait for you to learn about them.

Today is American Business Women’s Day, and I keep thinking about how recently women could be required to have a man’s signature to get a business loan.

Some states still required women to have a husband or other male relative co-sign a business loan until 1988?! What?! That was only 12 years before I started @spanx.

The progress came in steps. In 1974, the Equal Credit Opportunity Act made it illegal to deny women credit or require a male co-signer simply because they were women. Then, in 1988, the Women’s Business Ownership Act eliminated state laws requiring a husband or other male relative to co-sign a woman’s business loan - and expanded support for women entrepreneurs.

Not that long ago, a woman’s ability to access credit could depend on a man’s signature instead of her own ambition and ability to build. 🤯

Think of all the businesses, ideas, and inventions that may not have had the chance to exist before then.

I’m a big believer that the more women-owned businesses we have in this world, the better. ❤️

Tag a woman whose business you’re so glad exists. ⬇️

Hiring talented people is one of the easiest 10x-100x ROI opportunities.

And there’s always underpriced talent.
Price is what you pay. Value is what you get. Which means great value can still be a bad deal.

For all the talk of enterprise value and multiples, friendly reminder that it’s okay to just make money now. Sell some “unscalable” stuff for way more than it costs. Pocket the difference. Live your life.
Rather than buying things for less than their worth, make your brand so strong that when you buy something, it becomes more valuable by its association to you.

Pricing is the single strongest lever on profit in a business.

And yet - 95% of business owners look at what everyone else is charging, take the average, make that their price and never think about it again.

The problem is - the business owners they’re copying are broke too.

You want to sleep at night like you know everything is gonna work out.

And you want to wake up like there’s no chance it’ll happen unless you take relentless, unyielding, like-your-life-depends-on-it action.

If you’re not making money, it’s because:

You don’t know how to solve a valuable problem.
Or 
You can but no one knows about you.

That’s it.

Rule of life:

Never make asks of someone bigger than you. Give until they offer.

Just 6 years ago, my life looked very different than it does right now…and I have a video to prove it.

I was turning 52 and starting over.

Everything in my life had changed all at once.

My talkshow was canceled and I didn’t know my next career move.

My husband and I moved to Vermont and sold the home outside Boston where we had lived and raised our kids for 26 years.

I was living in a tiny town and had no friend group.

My body, my hormones, my routine and sense of self and purpose - gone.

It was almost as if I was stuck between two lives: the life I had been living and the life I had yet to create.

I started to convince myself at 52 that the best days of my life and career were behind me.

And that brings me to a video I want you to see.

It’s me on my 52nd birthday, crying alone in a bedroom describing how I feel.

Six years ago, there was no @themelrobbinspodcast .

There was no @letthemtheory book.

There was just me, starting over in a new chapter of my life and feeling scared and overwhelmed about all the unknowns.

And now here we are six years later.

Most people only know me because of what I’ve accomplished in the last four years (in my late 50s!)

You can change your life.

You can start exactly where you are and figure it out.

And if you keep waking up and moving forward and pushing yourself to try new things - over time you’ll surprise yourself.

Which is why I am waking up on my 58th birthday stunned by just how much my life has changed for the better.

If I can go from crying alone in a bedroom - to six years later changing every aspect of my life and myself - so can you.

And if you don’t believe in yourself right now, I want you to know that you can always borrow my belief in you, until you do.

Today I am doing chores in the most glamorous and expensive dress I own as a fun way to celebrate two amazing things happening this week:

1. It’s my 58th BIRTHDAY!!! (Or it was on the 6th…) - and I meant to post but I was enjoying the day with my family and never got around to it - so I’m telling you now!

2. The Mel Robbins Podcast is officially on the short list of 30 shows - who are invited to submit applications for the 2027 Golden Globes awards!!!!

In life, it is so important to stop and share good news with friends and family.

And it is also important to allow yourself to have some fun!

So, I pulled out the dress I wore as a nominee on last years red carpet (thank god it still fits) as a way to celebrate this amazing acknowledgment!

Congrats to everyone who made the Top 30!

But most importantly to all of our listeners around the world in 193 countries. Thank you for spending time with me and for sharing the episodes that inspire you with the people you love.

Keep those unpaid therapists in your life close… 

The friend who always knows exactly what to say and never judges, the coworker who can totally relate to everything you’re saying, the neighbor who notices when you need a boost…

They’re rare, they’re gold, and they deserve to know it.

🥲 so so surreal! i’ve watched Jimmy Fallon since I was a kid - him and his show are iconic in my eyes - and kids like me from Botswana / Plymouth in the UK don’t do Jimmy Fallon… I’m so grateful to my team, my family and to all of you guys for all the encouragement and support - today was another “wtf is going on..” moment ❤️👊🏾

Today was surreal! Prince William's team asked me to work with him over the coming years on a project to end homelessness in the UK through his Foundation @homewardsuk ! This is part of a multi-year campaign that me and Prince William are embarking on to change the state of homelessness in the UK.

🥪 We started the day in a Pret A Manger in Bournemouth! We both put on aprons, made coffee's, sandwiches, and got to meet some of the incredible team members that are former refugees, former inmates and formerly homeless!

⚽️ We drove over to Bournemouth FC and met players from the Men's and Women's team who had come through the bounce back program and used football to change their lives. 

🎤 I was lucky enough to have a few moments to ask the future king some questions on his own personal motivations and how we manages his time! 

👩🏻‍💼 Myself and Prince William then hosted a business round table with a group of local business leaders about how they could work to hire more homeless individuals into their organisation! 

This is just the beginning of a big piece of work we're planning to do with Prince William, Homewards and the UK business community to help get homeless people (and former inmates) back into work, to up-skill them and to end homelessness for good!

🤯 Side note:

If you had told me as a kid, I would be spending the day with Prince William, the future King - I would never ever ever believed you. I grew up with a Nigerian mother and a english dad who both adore the royal family, one of my earliest memories is watching my mum and dad cry when Diana died. William has a wonderful way with people, and he was authentically kind both on and off camera today! Thank you to whatever force in the universe put me there today, I'm so grateful and a little confused. A day I'm sure I'll tell my kids about. 

If you're a business please do check out Homewards work! Together as a business community we can do a lot more to get all the talent we have in this country back to work! ❤️

She said Yes 💍🥺

To say I was nervous is an understatement… i could feel my heart racing in my chest. She thought I was away in Europe - but I had snuck into Morocco on Christmas Day where she was on holiday with her family - I asked her mother and father if I could ask her to marry me - then had to build this big hut outside because a thunderstorm was forecast last minute 😅 - and then I stepped out and surprised her when she thought she was meeting her fam for dinner. Thankfully she said yes. 

10 years ago, I didn’t really understand the concept of marriage as many of you know - I was definitely an “avoidant” - but when you meet the right person, a lot of things start to make a lot of sense ❤️

Update: thank you for all the kind words and congratulations!!!

SOME NEWS 🚨 this year I’m joining @sharktankabc !!! 📺 🇺🇸 this was a dream of mine AND my mums...let me explain👇🏾

My nigerian mum raised 4 of us without being able to read or write herself, having left school when she was a child in Nigeria.

I struggled with school too - I wasn’t a smart kid and couldn’t pay attention, so I quickly realised the “traditional path” wasn’t going to work for someone like me

Then, when I was 12 years old, I discovered Dragons’ Den! 🐉

Me and my mum both fell in love with the show. Looking back, I think entrepreneurship offered us both hope - a path to a better life for people like us, who couldn’t pass tests in a classroom but were willing to work hard.

At 12 I would pause the TV and give my verdict, as if I was the 6th Dragon

By 16 I’d discovered Shark Tank and was starting my first (terrible) businesses

By 18 I was a university dropout with a start-up

And somehow, 9 years later, I ended up sitting in one of those Dragons’ Den chairs I used to shout at from our sofa

My mum has never fully gotten over it. 

When I call her today, 6 years later, the conversation is still 80% Dragons’ Den - her opinion on what I said, the businesses, what SHE would have done...

Btw, i’m genuinely not sure if she knows I have a podcast 😂 i don’t think she’s ever mentioned it 😅

But she knows Dragons’ Den, and that’s more than enough for her.

I know she’s always wanted me to do Shark Tank, so this phone call - telling her that day had come absolutely made my day, and hopefully her’s too!

I very much hope to do her proud + all of you that have supported me for the longest time... wish me luck!! 👊🏾❤️

P.S who would win in a fight, a shark 🦈 or a dragon 🐉 ???

linkedin.headline: Optimist, New York Times bestselling author of "Start with Why" and "The Infinite Game", and founder of The Optimism Company
linkedin.summary:
Simon Sinek is an unshakable optimist who believes in a bright future and our ability to build it together. Simon's WHY is to inspire people to do what inspires them so that, together, each of us can change our world for the better.

With a vision to change the way businesses think, act, and operate, Simon and his team work with leaders and organizations in nearly every industry to help transform company culture and create a better working world.

As a trained ethnographer, Simon has discovered remarkable patterns about how the greatest leaders and organizations think, act, and communicate. He is fascinated by the people and organizations that make the greatest, lasting impact on the world. He has devoted his life to sharing his thinking, and leading a movement to inspire people to do the things that inspire them.

Simon may be best known for popularizing the concept of WHY in his first Ted Talk in 2009. It has since become one of the most watched talks of all time on TED.com, with 37+ million views. 

Simon is a bestselling author and shares his ideas in the books Start With Why, Leaders Eat Last, Together Is Better, Find Your Why, and The Infinite Game.

Learn more at simonsinek.com.

The struggle is the point.

The process of figuring things out is what teaches us, fulfills us and, in the end, makes us happy. My fear is that AI makes it easy to skip that process entirely, including when we're trying to work through our own lives.

Harvard professor and happiness expert Arthur Brooks (@arthurcbrooks) is watching more of his students use AI as a therapist. His warning: it's built to tell you what you want to hear, not what you need to hear.

The people who help us grow are the ones who care enough to be honest with us.

This method from Cal Newport helped me figure out what I wanted to do with my life.

It's called values-centric lifestyle-based career planning. The idea is simple: work backwards from the lifestyle you want.

A lot of us think "I did a degree in X, so my only options are A, B, or C."

But actually, start by asking yourself what kind of life you want.

📅 What would your ideal week look like?

💸 What would you be doing if money were no object?

Most people get meaning from work. It's just that you'd probably be doing work you enjoy. So what would that look like?

Then based on that, figure out what kind of career would actually facilitate that lifestyle.

This advice really resonated with me when I was in med school.

🔍 Start with the life you want, then figure out the career that gets you there.

If you want to track where the 168-hours of your week goes, comment TIME for my free spreadsheet.

Someone asked: "My son just turned 22. What advice would you give him?"

Firstly, I don't give advice to people who aren't asking for it. So I probably wouldn't force my advice down your 22-year-old son's throat.

But if a 22-year-old came up to me and asked for general life advice, I'd say this.

When you're 22, you don't have a lot of experience in many things. You probably did something at university, maybe had some hobbies or side hustles, but you've got a fairly narrow range of stuff you've actually tried.

(P.S. Comment FOUNDATIONS below for my free 7-lesson course on how to build a $100k/year business)

So from 22 to 25, just try loads of things. Internships. Working for a small business. Random hobbies and side projects. Try learning the skills to make money independently on the internet.

And make sure you are creating more than you are consuming. Creating doesn't have to mean content. It can mean any form of making stuff and putting it out into the world.

Paul Graham has a great essay about finding work you love, and one of his guiding principles is "always be producing." The people who stumble into interesting careers tend to produce a lot. Most 22-year-olds I know spend 10 hours a day consuming content other people made.

Shift from consumer to creator. Try enough things and you'll eventually find the one where you're like "oh, I actually enjoyed that more than the others”, then narrow it down from there.

As Naval Ravikant says, find the thing that feels like play to you but looks like work to other people 🧙

EXCLUSIVE: Leave a “YES” below and I’ll DM you the full episode with @collingosselin1👇 Colin is shareing his story like never before on On Purpose 🎙️

Millions of people watched Colin grow up on Jon & Kate Plus 8. But what the cameras captured was only one version of his childhood. For the first time, Colin shares his account of what was happening behind the scenes—including childhood abuse, isolation, being institutionalized at 11 years old, and the years he spent trying to reclaim his life.

We talk about growing up without privacy, feeling unable to ask for help, being separated from his siblings, rebuilding his relationship with his dad, and the lasting impact of having your most formative years turned into entertainment for millions of people.

What stayed with me most was the purpose Colin has found through everything he’s experienced. Rather than allowing his past to define his future, he’s determined to use his story to advocate for children who may not have the ability or opportunity to speak for themselves.

If you’ve ever felt unheard, struggled to heal from your childhood, had to rebuild trust after being hurt, or wondered how to turn the most painful parts of your story into something meaningful… I hope this conversation reminds you that your past doesn’t have to decide who you become.

posts.caption:
When @MichelleObama and I were thinking about how to maximize our impact after leaving the White House, we landed on the idea of creating mentorship programs at the @ObamaFoundation. We wanted to invest in leaders around the world, just like people invested in us — helping them embrace broad perspectives, harness collective power, and drive meaningful change. 

We’re excited to introduce you to this year’s cohorts for our Obama Leaders Africa, Asia-Pacific, Europe, and USA programs. Some of them are students trying to find their place in the world, others are already on their way, with careers that span government, business, and civil society. But all of them have a shared commitment to create positive, sustainable change in their communities and around the world.

They join the members of our Voyager Scholarship with @BChesky and Obama Foundation Scholars program with the University of Chicago, and we can’t wait to see what they do!

Every part of your trip is now the easy part.
Starting today you can use Airbnb to:

• Connect with friends and get inspired
• Search in your own words
• Get to know a neighborhood before you book
• Compare homes side by side
• Find helpful services for a smoother stay

Not seeing something yet? Features are rolling out over time and may vary by location and device.

Today, @BarackObama, @MichelleObama and @BChesky, Airbnb co-founder and CEO, welcomed the fifth cohort of Voyager Scholarship recipients: 100 college juniors preparing for careers in public service.

The 2026–2028 class represents 39 states and territories and 68 colleges and universities. Sixty-one percent of the cohort are first-generation college students, bringing even more perspectives and lived experiences to the Voyager community.

Their work spans some of today’s most pressing challenges, from resilient infrastructure for island communities and water quality in the Great Lakes to accessibility policy for the Deaf community and the use of artificial intelligence in clinical care. Others are exploring graphic design as a tool for community engagement, first-time voter participation, food access in urban neighborhoods, and economic opportunity in rural and Appalachian communities.

“Every year, this scholarship reminds Michelle, Brian, and me that there is no shortage of young people ready to take on hard problems,” said President Obama. “This year’s Voyagers come from small towns and big cities, from islands in the Pacific and neighborhoods here on the South Side. They are working on housing, health care, clean water, and public safety, and most of them started that work long before anyone offered to pay for it. We’re proud to help them keep going.”

At the heart of the Voyager Scholarship is a shared belief that experiencing communities and cultures around the world can deepen understanding, build empathy, and prepare the next generation to create meaningful change.
Along with scholarship support, summer travel funding, and personalized career coaching, Voyagers participate in monthly virtual sessions where they sharpen their vision for a career in public service, strengthen their bridge-building skills, and build relationships with one another.

We can’t wait to see where their journeys take them. Join us in welcoming the newest class of Voyagers in the comments!

Just spent an amazing week in Mexico City with local Airbnb hosts, employees and partners.

We announced a MXN 20 million investment to expand Airbnb.org’s Medical Stays program to provide free Airbnbs for families traveling to Mexico City for lifesaving cancer care and other specialized treatments for their kids.

We also unveiled a free exhibition celebrating the history of the FIFA World Cup in Mexico, and an unbelievable Airbnb Experience hosted by the greatest Mexican football legend, @hugosanchez_9 

And I spent a lot of time with our incredible community of hosts. 90% of hosts here have one or two listings. 65% are women or seniors. 73% are hosting just to make ends meet. These hosts are some of the highest rated in the world, and represent the best of @airbnb 🇲🇽

The Obama-Chesky Voyager Scholarship invests not only in academic success, but in making meaningful work-travel experiences possible and helping to bring people together across their divides. ⁠

President Obama, Mrs. Obama, and Brian Chesky, Co-Founder and CEO of Airbnb, created the Voyager Scholarship because of a powerful idea: exposure to new places and experiences generates understanding, empathy, and cooperation, which equips the next generation to create meaningful change.⁠

Why @bchesky thinks that today’s AI models are more powerful than people realize

You belong in every room, and be shameless in asking for help, even from the president of the United States. That was the advice President @barackobama and Airbnb founder @bchesky , respectively, gave students from 71 colleges and universities during a conversation Monday with Foundation Executive Vice President of Programs Tina Tchen at an event at Home Court, one of the buildings at the Obama Presidential Center.

“I believe in paying dues and earning positions of authority and leadership and responsibility. And so I don’t want to be overconfident, but you should never feel as if … maybe you shouldn’t be there because your parents didn’t have a college education or because you’re a woman or because you’re a person of color. Because the truth of the matter is, and trust me on this one, I can say that I’ve met every titan of industry and every global leader of every sort and all the wealthy tech guys, and they were your age practically when they started,” said Obama during the conversation with recipients of the Obama-Chesky Scholarship for Public Service.

Later that day, President Obama met with students from @uchicago and @columbia who are part of the Obama Scholars program, to talk about global leadership and collaboration across areas of expertise.

From airbeds to 2 billion stays 🛏️

They threw three airbeds on the floor, built a website, hosted three strangers, paid the rent, and made friends. @airbnb was born. 

People told @bchesky the idea was crazy. Today it’s changed how the world travels. The lesson is simple. Start with what you have, test it in the real world, then scale what resonates. Curiosity and scrappy execution beat permission every time. 🙌🏽

This fall, join me for my @dailystoic Live speaking tour across the world. We’ll talk Stoicism and the practical ways you can apply it to the challenges you face day to day. I’ll even take your questions directly from stage.

Tickets are going fast—get yours at dailystoiclive.com or via the link in bio and grab one of the remaining VIP packages if you’d like to meet me before the show. I’ll see you out there.

I’ve written a lot of books. But this series — Courage is Calling, Discipline is Destiny, Right Thing, Right Now, and Wisdom Takes Work — is the one I’m most proud of. The one I believe matters most.

These books exist because I needed them. I needed to sit with these ideas, trace them back through history, find the people who actually lived them under pressure, and figure out what they meant for my own life.

The signed boxed set is available now at dailystoic.com/virtuesboxset or via the link in bio.

Australia & New Zealand — I’m coming back. 

This October, I’ll be returning for a 5-city tour to talk about Stoicism, discipline, leadership, and the lessons that have helped so many people around the world live a better life.

Whether you’ve read the books or listened to the podcast daily, I’d love to see you there to discuss these ideas in person. 

Sign up now for early access to tickets at dailystoiclive.com before they go on sale.

One of the beauties of traveling is being able to connect places with stories I’ve already read.

Here are some books related to my London trip.

This is one of my all time favorite books. The Harder They Fall by Bud Schulberg. For years, I thought of it as the book I read that spurred me immediately to quit my job in the corrupt, broken marketing world and to become a writer. But when I re-read it this year, I checked when I bought and first read it—2008. I didn’t leave the job for another THREE YEARS. Growth, it turns out, is always a slower, more incremental process than we think or rememer.

Maybe you can learn from my example and the cautionary tale that is this wonderful book, which we sell at The Painted Porch Bookshop.

Ryan Holiday acknowledges that his penchant for bidding on historically significant treasures has, at times, gotten out of hand. The best-selling author and ‘The Daily Stoic’ podcast host is roosting among his loot in his office above the Painted Porch Bookshop, the store he opened in 2021 in Bastrop, where he lives.

He loves objects that are “historical wormholes,” he says—things that make him “suddenly feel connected to the past.” In fact, the desk chair he sits in daily belonged to the late writer Joan Didion. The chair is hard wood and a bit uncomfortable for him, and it creaks whenever he leans back. It’s not ergonomic, but the best wormholes rarely are. Holiday won the chair in an auction after Didion’s death in 2021; he also bought her dining table and chairs, which he and his guests use when recording podcast episodes. (He restrained himself from purchasing Didion’s stately office desk, which ultimately sold for $60,000—“insanely expensive.”) 

Read more about Holiday’s treasures at the link in our bio.

“It’s my therapy,” says Debbie. 

At 69, she is still jumping at least once a month. 

It hasn’t been easy - and I jump with people who are in their 20’s who progress much faster than I do. But I keep pushing forward with my goals in mind. 

I can’t count the number of times I’ve told myself I should just quit. One of those times, I wrote down the benefits of skydiving for me. 

These are the positives that have come out of my skydiving experience, but it can apply to any sport. It’s not easy. It takes commitment and work. 

But the benefits are enormous:

I have to work out regularly & eat healthy to be able to do this.
I’m learning something new at this stage in life.
It’s a technical & physical challenge in freefall and canopy.
I’m constantly problem solving “on the fly”
I’m always striving to be better.
I feel better mentally & emotionally 
It gives me a great sense of accomplishment.
It has helped with my coordination & reflexes.
It keeps my brain and my body active.
It calms me.
I can be an inspiration to other women who think their lives are “over”

#itsnevertoolate and #wearenevertooold 

If this story inspired you please share 🙏💟

Stop making a 5 year plan. Do this instead. Tag someone who needs to hear it!

Every single action you take fundamentally changes the frontier of what’s possible next. Every door you walk through. Every skill you build. Every connection you make. Every new environment you enter.

New raw material creates new potential combinations, outcomes, and experiences. And perhaps most importantly, they compound. Each new skill, relationship, or experience doesn’t add one potential future, it multiplies them.

So, the real work isn’t planning your future, but building the frontier of what’s possible. It’s not asking yourself about your 5-year plan, but taking action to make the range of 5-year possibilities energizing.

So, stop trying to plan the perfect path.

You can’t plan for it. You don’t need to know where you’re going. You don’t need a map for your future.

You just need to take the next step. Use the three levers as a compass. Step with them in mind and the shadow future will expand and improve right in front of your eyes.

So, when a mentor asked me last week about my 5-year plan, I finally had an honest answer:

I don’t have one. And I’ve never been more energized about where I’m going.

Keep the compass. Burn the map.

That’s my rule. And I’m sticking to it.

What about you?

How you get your dopamine determines your outcomes. Choose wisely…

Dopamine from information gathering is a dangerous drug.

It’s the dopamine you get from reading. From planning. From learning. But never doing.

Information gathering as sport. Jammed into neat little dopamine feedback loops that convince you that you’re doing something productive and valuable.

You’re just one piece of information away from the big breakthrough. You’ll start when your business plan is perfected. You’ll meet your partner when you’ve scrolled through another round of profiles. You’ll get that dream job when you have one more degree in hand.

Your entire life will change when you realize the world isn’t run by a bunch of geniuses. The world is being run by a bunch of normal people with abnormal bias for action.

The answer you seek is hidden in the action you avoid.

Dopamine from information gathering is a dangerous drug.

Get your dopamine from action.

In 2021 @thechrisdo took my speaking fee from $1,000  to a $5,000 minimum. It wasn’t just a tactical adjustment. It was an identity shift 🤯

And I realized that is what I was missing all along. Did the strategies and tactics help me streamline my business? Absolutely. But I was missing an IDENTITY piece. I was missing the “I am worthy” piece of the puzzle 😭

Once I had that, I was actually able to implement more of the strategies Chris had given me content, branding, and lead generation over the years.

And that’s the thing I’ve learned most about, not only from the retreats and masterminds I’ve done with Chris. But that when we’re on the verge of EXPANSION or CHANGE, your subconscious mind is going to find a million ways to talk you OUT of taking the leap.

I don’t have the time.

Look closely at this photo. Notice what I'm doing???
It LOOKS like diligence... but it's actually AVOIDANCE.

I'm the one on the right, head down on my laptop at Chris Do's freaking Casa Dojo! It was the BEST SEAT I've ever had with him: extra time to talk and a REAL CHANCE at one-on-one coaching in person.

I've followed Chris for almost a decade and hosted him TWICE in Vancouver... Yet I STILL felt like I had to be on my best behavior around him.

So I retreated into the work. I polished a document. I cleaned up my prototypes. I packaged my business ideas.

It LOOKED like prudence.
It LOOKED like hard work.

But it was actually me avoiding LOOKING BAD.

Before the trip, I'd decided not to prepare. Chris even TOLD ME I just needed to show up. But by day 2, my old habits crept back in, and I wasn't listening.

That defeats the whole point of going. I came for coaching, and I was busy making sure I'd LOOK GOOD receiving it.

This is what PERFECTIONISM looks like. It doesn't look like panic. It looks like "discipline".

It's a pattern. Back in my engineering days, I'd take forever on technical reports, then be overly critical of every line. It slows my growth. The more reps I do, the better my quality gets. I've known that for a while, but KNOWING something and DOING it are two different things.

And here's what I missed in that room: the person across from you can only help with the REAL problem, NOT the polished version. I could have said, "This is where I'm at, and I don't know what to do. I need your help."

That's it.

Instead, I spent my best seat making sure I looked like I had it figured out.

Next time I catch myself polishing right before a conversation that matters, I'm going to say the MESSY version out loud first.

I'm still practicing.

Where in your work are you looking diligent when you're really avoiding?

Everything I'm building is exciting...That's exactly the problem.

Like a lot of creatives, I diverge. I explore. I chase the next shiny object because new territory is energizing. But at some point, everything on your plate is competing for the same finite energy.

When I was at @thechrisdo's business intensive at Casa Dojo, each of us got one hour of focused coaching on one big problem. Mine was this one: too many directions, and not enough clarity on which one to lean into.

So Chris had me lay out every initiative I'm running. Then he asked some questions that stood out for me:

1. Which one naturally energizes me?
2. Which one is the most scalable and sellable?
3. Which one supports my foundational income and cash flow?

After reflecting, I realized that those can be three different answers.

The one that lights me up isn't always the one that pays the bills. And the one that could sell someday might not be the one I want to spend my days on.

This is difficult because there's no single right answer... it depends on the season you're in.

- A season of profitability and scalability? Lean into what can grow and sell.
- A season of lifestyle and flexibility? Protect your energy and your time.
- A season of long-term building toward an exit? Invest in what compounds, even when it doesn't pay yet.

Although more ideas and more discipline would help, it wasn't what I needed. I needed someone to pull everything onto the table and reflect it back so I could see it clearly.

This is the biggest benefit that I've found in coaching and to have Chris filter my situation through his experience and lens was a huge privilege.

If you're a creative with too many things going on, try this: list everything you're working on, run each one through those three questions, and ask which season you're actually in.

Curious to know what season people are in right now...👇
